Nothing here is settled — and reviewing it is a short job

These are Marcus’s calls, not the band’s. Everything here was explored, measured and argued out, and Marcus picked a direction so the next stage wasn’t blocked. None of it has been through the band yet — so read it as a proposal with its reasoning attached, not as a decision you are being told about.

You are reviewing four choices: the wordmark, the skull, the typeface and the colour. Each is shown as it is now and as proposed, side by side, with one line on what changed. Everything else on this page is evidence of how those four behave once they are real, or the working-out that got to them — not thirteen more votes.

Short of time? Those four and stop. If you want the rules rather than the reasoning — which is what you need if you are about to make something rather than approve it — that is the guide.

In short

Six separate design explorations have run, and Marcus has picked a direction. The proposal: the logo is the word APEZONE in spaced-out capitals, drawn much heavier than the 2013 version, with the skull taken out of the word and given its own job.

And a fair amount of it now exists as real artwork. The wordmark, its dated version and the skull were drawn on 2 August — not concepts, not proxies — with the whole file set built from poster size down to the little icon in a browser tab. On 3 August the skull got a full-size treatment, the poster backgrounds were finished, and the profile pictures and headers for eight platforms were built.

How the page runs. Finished artwork first, then a line across the page, then the reasoning behind it. Nothing above that line is a concept — below it, assume a picture is one unless its caption says otherwise.

WHAT EXISTS

The finished artwork, all of it, in one place

Everything in this section is finished and usable tomorrow — and “usable” covers three different kinds of thing, which is worth saying because they are shown side by side. Most of it is artwork: a file built from a source drawing, sitting in this folder, that could go to a printer or onto a platform. The typeface is a licensed family, chosen and subset rather than drawn. The palette is seven numbers rather than a file at all. All three are settled, and each card says which it is.

All four of the choices you are reviewing appear here — the wordmark, the skull, the typeface and the colours — alongside the things built on top of them.

Three honest caveats, and they apply throughout. These are screen renders — with one exception: the test sheets were printed twice on 3 August on an office machine, which is a sanity check rather than a proof, and is why two of these pictures changed. Where a card shows a composed poster, the finished file is usually the element on it rather than the whole sheet: the poster is there so you can see what the element is for. And this is one picture per piece, not per file — the logo alone is 98 exports across every size, colour and format, and showing them all would tell you nothing.

The palette — seven values

Not a file — seven numbers, and they are what a printer, a merch supplier and a website all have to be given. Two hues only: one cold at 201° across five values, one warm at 40° across two. Every pair that carries text has been checked for contrast by calculation rather than eye. The gold is the one that will disappoint in print unless it is specified as a spot colour — that is unproven and it is why nothing has been ordered.

THE STARTING POINT

Four identities, and the one thing they share

Before any of the new work makes sense, this is what it is measured against. Apezone has had four distinct visual identities, and they have almost nothing in common with each other — different palettes, different logic, and in two of the four, no skull at all.

The earliest two were only recovered from the Internet Archive on 31 July 2026. Nobody had seen them in twenty years, and finding them changed the plan: the archive was supposed to confirm that the skull was the band’s one constant. It isn’t.

1999–2003 Hazard signs and apes The Unbalanced EP cover. Yellow, black and red, a warning triangle, and a joke in the artwork. No skull anywhere — it does not exist yet.
2011–2012 The badge Skull on a red disc, stars either side, APEZONE arched above and B.A.M.F. below. Black, red, grey, white. Sticker-and-patch logic. The skull was drawn by Juha Syrjänen of Honey Hellraiser — a favour, for the B.A.M.F. EP — and the band evolved it from this point.
2013 Stripped to a wordmark The skull leaves the primary mark and comes back as the O, in red. The letters are hairline-thin and very widely spaced.
2015 Art Nouveau Ornate monoline lettering, skull back inside the O, floral scrollwork, blackletter titles. Cold slate blue-grey on near-black, and no red at all.
2027 What is proposed The same seven letters, spaced the same way — drawn about twice as heavy, with the O a plain ring and the skull promoted out of the word into its own two jobs.
What actually survives all four

The word, spaced out. Not the skull. APEZONE in widely letterspaced capitals appears on the 1999 gig poster, the 2001 website, the 2013 album cover and the 2015 site — every era, start to finish, and still the band’s mark today. The ape theme goes back to the beginning; the ape skull only arrives in 2011, twelve years in.

That single finding is why the proposal is wordmark-led, and why the skull gets promoted to its own job rather than being made to carry the name. Every start-and-end pair below follows from it.

The 2013 and 2015 marks are the band’s own files and recovered web assets. The last card is a weight proxy, not artwork — the 2013 outlines mechanically thickened to the specified weight, which is a fair guide to mass and to nothing else.

THE PROPOSAL

The name, set in type

The proposed arrangement: the seven letters, spaced out, with a plain ring for the O and no skull inside the word.

Where we started 2013 — the band’s own file

Hairline geometric capitals with a red skull standing in for the O. The skull is the only thing on the line with any mass, so it shouts while the type whispers. Measured, the strokes are about 12% of capital height.

Where we ended up 2026 — the finished drawing

The same seven-letter arrangement, at 24% — roughly twice the stroke. The skull is gone from the word and the O is a plain ring. The spacing was rebuilt for an even rhythm. This is the real artwork, not a proxy.

What changedThe arrangement was already right and the band arrived at it twice on their own. What changes is weight, and the skull leaving the word. At the old thickness the name reads as composed and carries no signal at all; drawn heavy it changes register completely, and that single change is what stops it being anonymous.
Two details worth knowing

The A keeps its pointed top with no crossbar. That is the band’s own 2013 letterform and the only part of those letters with real character. It costs a small pause on first reading — some people see a Greek lambda before they see an A — and that was judged worth keeping deliberately.

The weight is most of the point. At the old thin weight the word is composed and carries no signal at all — it could be a skincare brand. Drawn heavy, it changes register completely. That single change is what stops the logo being anonymous.

THE SKULL

Promoted, not demoted

The skull comes out of the word, and that is a promotion rather than a demotion. It gets two jobs instead of one cramped one.

  • Big: the band’s illustration — posters, sleeves, shirts, back patches. Drawn in detail, at a size where detail actually reads.
  • Small: a stripped-down version for profile pictures, the browser tab and app icons. This is the jawless skull that came out of round B.

The reason it could not stay inside the O is mechanical: welding it into a capital letter permanently sizes it to a capital letter, and that is the one place it cannot afford to be small. What makes it read as an ape rather than a generic skull is a ridge along the top of the cranium, and that ridge needs room.

That argument did not survive. It is kept here because it is why the skull left the letter — and that part still holds — but the ridge itself has since gone from every version of the mark. What replaced it as the ape cue is the shape of the brow and the cheekbones, and at the smallest sizes the honest answer is that it reads as a fanged skull rather than specifically an ape one.

Where we started 2012 — drawn by Juha Syrjänen

The complete drawing: cranium, brow, cheekbones, muzzle, upper teeth and the full lower jaw. Not the band’s own hand — Juha Syrjänen of Honey Hellraiser drew it as a favour for the B.A.M.F. EP, and the band evolved it from there. Genuinely good, and unmistakably an ape rather than a human. But it is drawn in negative — the lines are the gaps between white shapes — so shrinking it closes the gaps before the shapes, and the bottom half fills in solid. The silhouette is a wide X, thrown out sideways by the cheekbones.

Where we ended up the finished drawing, on a dark background

The shape stops at the brow: no cranium, no jaw. The cheekbones pull in, so it fits a square rather than a butterfly. Two canines hang free and nothing else needs explaining. This is the real file, not a concept. On a light background the same drawing appears as dark linework instead — it is one two-tone artwork, and whichever tone matches the background disappears. But it is a different drawing, not the old one edited: its outline was rebuilt from a machine-generated image and corrected, with Juha’s eye sockets placed into it.

What changedEverything except the face came off. Not for style — the top of the head was drawn as an outline with nothing inside it, so on this identity’s near-black ground it was invisible, and on a bright one it came back as horns. Seven ways of fixing it were drawn and the answer was to delete it. Marcus’s call, and the reason is the good bit: the ape has no jaw anyway, so it makes sense only the front is visible. A fragment, twice, for the same reason. One caveat, kept in view rather than buried: the drawing that had the invisible top was already on its way out, so applying the decision to the drawing that stays means removing a top that currently works. Spelled out below.
And one drawing became two

The old file had to be a poster and a favicon, and could only manage the first. It is now two drawings: the detailed one above for print and merch, and a separate, simpler one for profile pictures and browser tabs. Splitting the job is what let the small one give up detail it could not afford — it still reads at 16 pixels, where the old drawing had gone to mush well before that. Both are shown below.

The family still doesn’t quite match — and here is why

Taking the top of the head off was decided for the big skull, and it now applies to the small one too. What did not work was making the big drawing itself shrink — so the identity is two related drawings that change over at 48 pixels, both of them front-of-the-face with no top of the head.

The reason is worth knowing, because it is not a matter of taste. In the big drawing the eye sockets are gaps between strokes; in the small one they are holes. Shrink a hole and it is still a hole; shrink a gap and it closes. So the big skull genuinely cannot be made tiny, whatever is done to it. The skull, at every size has the comparison, and it is not close.

The big skull lost the top of its head — deliberately

One of the skull drawings had a problem nobody had spotted: the top of the skull was drawn as an outline with nothing inside it, so on the near-black background this identity uses, it was simply invisible. Put it on a bright or busy background and it came partly back — as two pointed corners that read as horns.

Seven ways of fixing it were drawn. The answer was to delete it. The mark becomes the front of the skull — no jaw, no cranium. Marcus’s call, and the reason is the good bit: the ape has no jaw anyway, so it makes sense only the front is visible. A fragment, twice, for the same reason.

An honest wrinkle worth knowing

The drawing with the invisible top is the one in the background mockups — and it had already been set aside by the review, in favour of a more detailed drawing. Both of the drawings that are actually specified were then checked, and neither has the problem: in both, the top of the skull is a solid shape.

So the fault belonged to one drawing that was on its way out. The decision does not. “Only the front of the skull is visible” is a choice about what shape the mark is, and it carries over — but applied to the final drawing it meant removing a top that currently worked, and losing the ridge with it. That was a bigger call, and it was worth making deliberately rather than inheriting.

Made, and then made twice more. The top of the head was tested again in August as a solid rounded shape rather than an outline — it genuinely helps at tiny sizes, and it still reads as a hat, so it went. And on 3 August the small drawing’s own ridge came off too. No version of the mark now has anything above the brow. Three attempts, three rejections.

Still unresolved — how the big skull is actually drawn

The shape is now fully agreed, top included. How it gets rendered at poster size is not. Every version so far is flat line art, which reads as a sticker rather than as an object once it is big. It needs real dimension — planes, light, material.

Attempts to add that by processing the existing drawings have failed, for a reason worth knowing: depth has to be drawn in, it cannot be added afterwards. So it gets its own round before anyone draws the final artwork. That work is briefed and not started.

TYPOGRAPHY

The typeface — everything that isn’t the logo

The wordmark is drawn by hand. But everything around it — song titles, gig listings, the website, the press kit — needs a typeface. The choice, approved by Marcus and reviewable like everything else here, is one family doing both jobs: Barlow. The typography report has the measurements and the runners-up.

The specimen below is set in the real thing. It is embedded in this page, so what you are reading is the actual typeface, not a picture of it.

Where we started the old identity — SF Movie Poster

The display face used across the poster-era material, set here in the same words as the specimen below. It has no real lowercase: the “small” letters are just capitals at 75% height, checked in the font file. So it can head a poster and it can do nothing else — there was never a text face to go with it.

Where we ended up proposed — Barlow, live on this page
THIRTY YEARS
OF APEZONE
The back catalogue is going up
26.02.1999  ·  Karkkila, Rautaruukki

One family covering both jobs, in four weights. Its heavy weight measures 26.9% stroke thickness against the logo’s 24%, so it sits beside the mark without competing — and its regular weight sets running text, gig dates and Finnish letters properly.

What changedFrom a display face with nothing behind it to a system. The old face could set a poster headline and then ran out; everything else — a gig list, a biography, a website — had to borrow a typeface from somewhere, which is why the old material never looks like one thing. The point of choosing Barlow is not that it is prettier. It is that there is now one answer for all of it.

Founded at Easter 1997 in Cafe Maestro, Helsinki, by two people who decided to start a band while comfortably drunk. Thirty years later it is still going. The palette is cold with a single warm note; the type is meant to get out of the way and let the mark carry the weight.

Why this one
  • It doesn’t fight the logo. Its heavy weight measures 26.9% thickness against the logo’s 24% — close enough to sit beside it without competing. Heavier faces out-muscle the mark; lighter ones go thin and boutique.
  • It comes from signage. Road signs, number plates, transit — which is the register the identity is after, without being a literal copy of a traffic font.
  • Finnish works properly. ä ö å Ä Ö Å are all well drawn, which is not a given. PÄIVIÖ, JYVÄSKYLÄ and HYVINKÄÄ all set cleanly.
  • Numbers line up in columns — which matters more than it sounds for gig lists and a discography.
  • It’s free and self-hosted. Open licence, four files, about 127 KB total. No subscription, and nothing phoning home to Google.
The honest weakness

Barlow’s normal weight is the lightest of the faces tested. At 16 pixels light-on-dark it holds; below 14 it starts to thin out. The fix is a rule — step up one weight for anything very small — but if the website ends up with a lot of small text, the runner-up (Archivo, with a sturdier body face) is worth revisiting before building.

Swapping is a one-session job and nothing else in the identity moves.

COLOUR

Two colours, and one of them barely appears

Near-black ground, bone-coloured text, and a single warm gold used very sparingly. That is the whole system — one cold colour family and one warm one, nothing else.

Where we started 2011–2012 — sampled off the badge
Black#231F20
Signal Red#BF1E2D
Shadow Red#6F0E10
Mid Grey#C0BEBF
Deep Grey#747273
White#FFFFFF

Four colours doing unrelated jobs, plus two shadow tints. Red is the loudest thing in the identity and it is used as decoration rather than for anything in particular. The 2013 and 2015 eras then each replaced the palette outright rather than developing it — three palettes in four years.

Where we ended up proposed — two hues, six values
Ink#0A1116
Slate#1B2830
Steel#3F5260
Bone#C6D2D6
Aged Brass#9C7C3C
Lamp Amber#D9B36A

One cold hue at four values and one warm hue at two, plus Paper for print. That structure is lifted from the 2015 EP, which the measurement showed was a single hue at four or five values with no outlier anywhere — the one piece of real discipline in the band’s colour history.

What changedRed is out, and the structure is inherited rather than invented. Red was made to compete against three non-red candidates and lost on arithmetic: on the near-black ground this identity actually uses, a red muted enough to be tasteful scores 2.48:1 against the 4.5:1 that text needs. The band had already stopped using it in 2015; this makes that permanent.
Ink#0A1116The ground. Almost everything sits on this.
Slate#1B2830Raised panels and surfaces.
Steel#3F5260Graphic mass and rules. Never text.
Bone#C6D2D6Text, and the logo when reversed.
Aged Brass#9C7C3CThe one warm colour. Used sparingly.
Lamp Amber#D9B36AThe brighter version, dark grounds only.
Paper#F2F1EEFor print and anything on white stock.
Why there is no red

Red had to earn its place against non-red alternatives, and it lost on measurement rather than taste. A deep oxidised red on the near-black ground the brand actually uses scores 2.48:1 for contrast — well below the 4.5:1 needed for text to be reliably readable. So it could never carry a link, a date or a caption; it would be decoration only.

And muted enough to be readable, it stops being warmth — it reads as a stain rather than as heat. A red saturated enough to do the job is the 2011 red, which the identity is deliberately moving away from.

One practical warning for merch

Gold-family colours reproduce badly in standard four-colour printing — they go flat, dull and slightly green. For anything printed where the gold matters, a spot colour has to be specified and proofed first. This is the single most likely disappointment in the whole palette, and it is cheap to avoid by planning for it.

THE WHOLE SYSTEM

Six elements, and they are not equals

Four choices are being reviewed above. This is how they sit together with the two secondary devices and the release signs — and it matters because the gallery near the top shows every finished piece at the same size, which makes them look like equals. They are not. The wordmark is the identity; everything else supports it, decorates around it, or belongs to one campaign.

The one that catches people

The skull is not the logo. It is the band’s illustration, and it has been since the direction was settled. Anybody meeting the skull first — on an avatar, on a plate, on a shirt — reasonably assumes otherwise, and an outside reviewer reading these pages did exactly that. The word is the logo. The skull is what the word’s band draws.

And one large-format element per surface — rings or shards or a full-bleed photograph. Never two, for the same reason the palette allows one warm element.

THE OTHER ELEMENTS

Two things that aren’t the logo, and are keepers

Round C explored well beyond the logo, and two of the things it made survived the review — not as marks, but as elements the brand can use. Both come with hard rules about where they may appear, because both fail if used wrongly.

Why the rings are kept — and the rule attached

The review’s words: at hero size it is the most beautiful object round C produced, and it is beautiful because it is true. If you measure the rings, the data holds up. If you never notice the encoding, it still works as pure proportion.

Large format only. Tested down a size ramp it dies — a visible moiré rosette by 96 pixels, a fuzzy donut by 48. So: website hero, anniversary poster, vinyl label, stage backdrop. Never a logo, never small. And it carries its one-sentence explanation once, somewhere findable — not repeated everywhere.

These exist now, and Marcus changed them twice on the way
  • They were built grey first. A palette rule caps the gold at 2% of any surface, so the first version had none — and next to the original sketches it was clearly the wrong picture. That rule turned out to be about a highlight, not a background. Marcus chose gold, and the rule now says so in writing.
  • They were built as drawings first, too, and that lost as well. These are generated images, like the originals were — and then every pixel is snapped onto the five brand colours, which is what makes one a brand asset instead of just a nice picture. It also removes something important: the generator’s gold drifts orange, and this brand allows no red at all. Measured before the snap: up to 2.3% red. After: zero.
  • They were too dark at first, and had a hole in the middle. Marcus again: the first gold version was “a bit boring, as they only have one color”. Measured, it was 14% light against 73% near-black, where the originals he likes are about 42% light — cream has to be a main colour, not a highlight. And the dark middle is gone: it used to be painted into the artwork, which decides forever where a logo may sit. Now the field runs edge to edge, and the dark middle is added only where there is type to protect.
  • Type on top needs a real dark wash behind it, and now that is proven. The old sketch claimed one and never had it. On gold it matters much more: pale letters straight onto a gold shard are invisible, and all 100 test placements failed without the wash. With it, none did.
  • No stars, and nothing else gold on the same surface. The field is the warm thing; everything set on it is pale grey.
PUT TOGETHER

The logo and the layout grammar, on the same page

Everything so far has been judged on its own — the logo against a plain background, the layout grammar on posters with no logo on them at all. Look back at the poster in the previous section: the band’s name at the bottom is typed, because when it was made there was nothing to place there.

So the two had never been in the same frame. That was the last thing the wordmark owed, and it is now done: the same poster rebuilt with the real logo dropped in, plus the image a shared link shows.

Where we started the layout, with no logo

The name at the foot is set in a placeholder typeface, because in October there was no drawing to use. Everything else — the line along the top, the date as the hero, the activity strip — is the grammar being proposed.

Where we ended up the same poster, real logo in place

A3, at the size it would actually print. The typed name is gone and the drawn one is there instead, and the grey body text is now the same off-white as everything else — that grey was too faint against the near-black to be legal, which nobody had checked.

What changedThey get along. The worry was that a heavy logo would crowd a layout designed around empty space. It doesn’t — but it had to be made roughly twice the size the placeholder was. Thin spaced-out letters and a solid drawn logo do not occupy a page the same way, and matching their width does not match their presence.
Why there is no writing on it

A link image is a single fixed picture, but every app decides for itself how big to show it — full width in a browser, a thumbnail in a chat. The picture cannot respond. Anything small enough to be a caption at full size is unreadable in a chat preview, and unlike a website it cannot drop it.

So the link image carries the logo and the strip. The strip is the thirty years — one mark per year since 1997, the last one hollow because it hasn’t happened — which says the anniversary without spelling it.

Three things this turned up
  • The old poster quietly broke two of its own rules. It had two warm accents where the rule allows one, and set three lines in a grey that fails against the background. Both were caught by measuring the finished picture rather than reading the code, and both are fixed here.
  • On the dark background there is exactly one legal colour for text — the off-white. Everything else is either too faint or is the accent, which is capped at 2% of any surface. Emphasis has to come from size and weight alone.
  • Don’t put the top line next to the logo. That line starts with the word APEZONE, so beside the logo the page says the name twice, 100 pixels apart. At opposite ends of a poster it reads like a masthead and an imprint and is fine. Side by side it reads like a mistake.

These two are renders — the sheets that were printed in August were the large-format ones, not these — and the poster copy is placeholder. The date on it is not a gig.

IN USE

Which version goes where

One of the more useful outcomes: instead of one logo stretched across every job, there is a small family, and each member has a defined size range. This is why a logo that looks fine on a poster does not have to also survive being 16 pixels wide in a browser tab.

VersionUsed atWhere you’d see it
The skull, detailedLarge / printPosters, sleeves, shirts, back patches
The wordmark120px wide and upWebsite header, video titles, letterhead
Wordmark + 1997–2027240px wide and upAnniversary material. Below that, drop the date rather than shrink it
The small skull24–96pxProfile pictures, avatars, small merch
The small skull, again24px and underBrowser tab, app icon

The wordmark stops at 120 pixels for a simple reason: seven spaced-out letters cannot fit into a browser tab. No amount of skill fixes that, which is why the skull has to carry the small sizes on its own.

Where this now stands

Phase 2 is finished. The word, the skull, the colours, the typeface, the art direction and the guide that pulls them together are all done, and the files are built. Nothing in the identity is blocking the press kit, the merch artwork or the website any more.

What is left in Phase 2 is not work, it is looking: nobody has seen the tab icon in a real browser tab. STILL OPEN

What is not decided — and what just closed

The band hasn’t reviewed any of it Everything above is Marcus’s pick. It was chosen against written reasoning rather than taste, but it has had exactly one person’s judgement applied. This is the review.
Who draws it — answered Nobody, in the sense of hiring anybody. No designer, nothing drawn by hand — the files get produced with the software and AI tooling Marcus already has. That works because the job isn’t illustration: the drawing exists, and what remains is arithmetic on it — reduce, respace, thicken, crop. This was the last thing holding up the redraw.
Juha Syrjänen’s blessing — got it The skull was drawn by Juha Syrjänen of Honey Hellraiser, as a favour, for the B.A.M.F. EP. He’s happy for the band to do what they like with it and wants no say in what it became. So this one is closed rather than open — it’s here because he should be credited, and because it means the original file is gone and the archive is all there is.
The skull — drawn, and it ships Finished on 2 August, and it took giving up on the top of the head for the third time: every version drawn read as a helmet or a bread roll rather than as bone. So the big skull is the front of the face only. It exists at every size from poster down to browser tab. The skull, at every size is the detail.
…but as two drawings, not one Below 48 pixels the identity uses round B’s simpler skull. Both are the front of the face with no top of the head, so they are close relatives — but they are two files, not one. The detailed drawing genuinely cannot be made that small — its eye sockets are gaps between strokes rather than shapes, and a gap just closes up. This is the one thing the last round set out to fix and didn’t. The real fix is redrawing the big skull with closed eyes and nose, which would mean throwing away the drawing just approved.
Does it look like anyone else’s? — tested, and it holds The test was deliberately changed. Setting it against other rock bands’ logos would have been a win by default — that genre runs on gothic lettering and spikes, and this is neither. So it was set against the real risk instead: the same word in five ordinary spaced-out capital typefaces, matched for size. It is pickable out of the line-up instantly. But the thing doing that work is almost entirely the pointed A — cover it and the rest is close to an off-the-shelf typeface. Which makes that letter a do not change this, not a detail. The literal side-by-side against other bands’ artwork was not run; it would mean pulling their files into the project.
The logo and the layout grammar together — proved The last thing the word owed. The poster and the link image above are the first artefacts in this whole project with both the real logo and the layout system in the same frame — everything before was one or the other. They get along; the logo just has to be drawn about twice the size the placeholder was.
Gold in print Still unproofed, but no longer unseen: on an office printer the gold does read as gold. Two things to watch on a real proof — the darker brass went a little olive, and the two darkest greys were almost impossible to tell apart. Needs a spot-colour match before any merch or print commitment.
The browser-tab check — the one thing the logo still owes Every size claim in this whole project is a computer render. The 16-pixel icon has never been seen in an actual browser tab, next to ordinary ones, by anybody who hasn’t been staring at it. The test now ships with the files and takes one command. Nothing else about the mark is outstanding.
Has anyone else got this skull? The word was checked against look-alikes; the skull was not. It matters more here, because the outline was rebuilt from an image a machine generated in an earlier round rather than drawn from the band’s own file.
The teasers are in colour — and they are not graded The photographs are black and white; the videos are not. Marcus’s call. So the question became whether to process them, and the answer is no: there has never been a specification for what a colour Apezone picture looks like, so inventing one now would be designing rather than filming. But “leave it as is” is a trap — a phone hands you its grade whether you asked or not: saturation up, contrast up, sharpening, and a white balance that wanders between shots. So the work moves to the moment of filming: lock the white balance, turn the phone’s “enhance” off, lock the exposure. Afterwards, fix the white balance if it drifted and nothing else. And still turn the coloured bulb off — in black and white a red-lit room was unusable, and in colour it is just red all over, which is worse.
Colour video and the one colour rule — settled The palette has one hard rule: no red, anywhere. That was free while the videos were black and white. It stopped being free the moment they went to colour, because a camera pointed at a real rehearsal room records a red amp light, a red cable, somebody’s red shirt. Settled by Marcus on 4 August: the rule covers the colour the band chooses, not the colour the room happens to be. So no red brought in on purpose, no grading toward red, and no frame that is red all over — but a red plectrum is just a red plectrum. And on anything the brand puts on top of the footage — an end card, a caption — the rule stays absolute. The footage is a record; the graphics on it are the brand. Settled with three days to spare before the first rehearsal.
The gag question — settled Two of the band’s own rules pointed opposite ways: the art direction bans visual gags outright, and the brand platform says videos are where the humour lives. Both are Marcus’s, both from the same week. The line between them: the camera never tells the joke, but the band can. Everything on the banned list — a banana, a gorilla suit, ape hands — is something somebody has to bring. Nothing stops five people who have known each other for thirty years being funny in a room, and a frame that couldn’t hold that has already gone too solemn. What is out is the edit doing it: no zoom-in, no freeze-frame, no boing.
The warning sign is coming back — Manu, Jukka and Tuomas to confirm The 1999 Unbalanced sleeve was a yellow warning triangle with a figure slipping over, punning on the title. It is being revived as one sign per release — falling rocks for Get Stoned With Alexis, a sunrise for Tomorrow Is A New Day. Marcus has agreed; he also pointed out that the joke is from before he joined, so the three who made it should see it first. Worth being clear what is being agreed to: not a style, but a promise that every future record has an idea that can be drawn as a road sign.
Which Nummela photographs are Apezone? Apezone played Nummela in 2012 as the warm-up for Honey Hellraiser — so the shoot covers two bands and a whole evening, across 197 photographs. It is the best live photography the band has, and it processes beautifully. None of it can be used until somebody who was there says which frames are which. Worth an hour.
The photographs were too dark — fixed The first version of the art direction processed every picture onto the brand’s dark colours and capped how bright it could get. On a dark page that made everything recede. Marcus called it, and the numbers agreed: one frame had less contrast against the page than a button is required to have. Photographs now run from true black to true white, and a photographer who already grades well is left alone. A colour version was built and tested too; he preferred black and white.
Most of the 2011 live photographs are unusable Not a judgement — a measurement. They were shot under red and magenta stage wash, and once the colour is taken out there is nothing underneath: the person is a silhouette in front of a blown-out lamp. Worth knowing before anyone plans something around old photographs.
Nobody outside this folder has seen any of it The honest gap, and it took an outsider to name it. Everything here has been checked against itself — contrast maths, minimum sizes, print tests, and a line-up against rival marks. None of it has been shown to a single listener. So the plan now carries one cheap test: show ten to fifteen people the wordmark, the skull, a poster and the shirt for five seconds each, with no explanation, then ask what kind of band they think it is, what era, and what they remember. It runs before anything is printed, because a print run is expensive to regret and this is an afternoon with a phone. It is evidence, not a vote — the decisions stay in the band.
BEFORE YOU JUDGE IT

What none of this is yet

The dividing line is the one across the page near the top. Above it, everything is finished artwork. Below it, most pictures are not — they are still here because they are the argument, but they are not the outcome:

  • Finished, and safe to use: everything in What exists — the wordmark and its dated version, the skull at both sizes, the two engraved plates, the gold fields, and the profile set for eight platforms. All built from source drawings and measured against the specification. Judge these as final.
  • Concepts, and several of them rejected: the skull images in the round sections — traced versions of machine-generated attempts, kept to show what was compared against what.
  • Candidates, not assets: the three other skull materials — bone, granite, cast. Each needs the skull to be allowed a third shade of grey, which is Marcus’s call and has not been made. Only the engraving ships.
  • The detailed specimen images are pastiche of an object that does not exist.
  • The skull’s origins are a weaker story than the word’s. Its outline was rebuilt from a machine-generated image and corrected, rather than drawn from the band’s own file. Nobody has yet checked it against existing marks.

Almost nothing here has been seen on paper, at physical size, or on a real phone. Nearly every size claim on this page is a computer render — including, still, the browser-tab icon. The exception is the engraved skull, which was the one most likely to change on press and duly did: printed at four widths, its fine crossed lines close up into a grey smudge below about 42 mm. It now has a size limit and a plain-drawn alternative for anything smaller.

That is what a phase like this produces. It only becomes a problem if someone mistakes one of the rejected concepts below for a finished piece — which is what the line across the page is for. If it is above the line, it is real; if it is below, read the caption.

Big enough for a wall

Two things made for the sizes where detail finally survives — a poster, a shirt back, the top of a website. The skull got given a material: four were tried, and the one that shipped is the old natural-history-plate treatment, drawn in fine lines rather than shaded, because it is the only one that keeps the skull to its two allowed colours. And a long-standing promise about keeping small text readable over a busy background was finally measured instead of assumed — it failed, and had to be rewritten before it passed. The backgrounds themselves got rebuilt twice after Marcus said the first versions had lost what he liked about the originals: they are gold now, and generated rather than drawn. Then Marcus printed it, and the paper found two things no measurement had: the fine-line skull dies somewhere under 42 mm wide, and the dark wash behind the type had been quietly eating a whole corner of the gold. Both fixed — and the reprint found a third thing, which only became visible once the gold was back: the wash over the middle was leaving a grey stain. It is lighter now.

Both shipped. Printed twice.

the year rings — and the one thing you can put on a shirt

Thirty years, drawn as rings

One ring for every year since Easter 1997, each one thicker the more the band did that year. Count them and the biography checks out. It came out of round C and had been sitting in a folder ever since; Marcus asked for it as real files, “especially clothing” — and that turned out to be the reason it had to be this one. The gold broken-glass backgrounds are AI-generated, and their licence will not let a generated image be the main picture on something you sell. These rings have no generated anything in them, so they are the only large piece of artwork the band can actually put on a shirt front. Getting them ready found three faults nobody had noticed in four days of liking the picture. The worst: the 2027 ring is supposed to be a hollow ring, meaning ‘this has not happened yet’ — and it was drawn solid. In colour the amber carries the meaning. In one colour, which is what a printed shirt is, it came out exactly as thick as a year with one gig in it. The drawing was telling a lie. It is a real hole now. Also measured for the first time: how big it has to be printed — and the limit comes from the empty years, whose rings are the thinnest lines in the whole picture.

Decided. Nothing printed.

Not the logo — the pictures. Worked out by processing the band’s own old photographs rather than by collecting other people’s, which turned up something an opinion would have missed: a photograph taken under coloured stage lighting cannot be rescued, so white front light has to be asked for when the gig is booked.

Black and white, and bright.

HOW IT GOT HERE

Six design rounds — and what didn’t survive

Background, not conclusions. These six are the working-out. Parts of every one of them were overruled, and one of them — round D — concluded that nothing it produced was worth keeping. Read them if you want to know why a decision went the way it did. Skip them entirely and you miss nothing about the brand itself: that is all in the documents above.

The rounds were run deliberately independently. Where two of them disagreed, that was treated as useful information rather than as a problem to smooth over — and the disagreements are where most of the good decisions came from.

A separate review then weighed all of them against the agreed positioning and settled the conflicts. It overruled parts of every round, including two of Marcus’s own picks, and argued each of those in the open rather than quietly.

logo & colour

The first full exploration. Measured the band’s own 1997–2015 material rather than working from taste, and proposed the letterspaced APEZONE wordmark with the skull taken out of the word.

Its main direction won.

The big skull’s cranium vanished on a dark background and came back as horns on a bright one. Seven ways of fixing it were drawn — and the measurement showed the top of the head had never been visible in the first place.

Wordmark treatments

What if the name were chrome, or gold foil, or neon, or pressed into paper? Twenty-six versions were drawn, then ten more were made with an AI image tool to see whether it could do better. It could not. Every AI version quietly redrew the letters — changing their shapes, their spacing, and in one case adding a bar across the A that our A has never had.

The drawn ones won.

Round G

Round F never tested a complete skull — none existed. This round generated twenty-three of them, top of the head and jaw included, anchored on the band’s own drawings, and measured them against the front-only version. The jaw never once came back calm: it arrived snarling, or cute, or not at all.

The fragment held. Confirmed.

GLOSSARY

The handful of words that keep coming up

Lockup
A fixed arrangement of elements that always go together — here, the word and sometimes the date. You do not rearrange a lockup; you place it.
Glyph
The stripped-down small version of the skull. Simple enough to survive being tiny.
Favicon
The tiny icon in a browser tab. Usually 16 pixels — smaller than most people realise, which is why it drives so many decisions.
Vector
Artwork stored as shapes rather than pixels, so it scales to any size without going fuzzy. A real logo has to be vector.
Reverse / positive
Reverse is light artwork on a dark ground; positive is dark on light. This identity is reverse by default.
Contrast ratio
A measured number for how readable one colour is on another. 4.5:1 is the accepted minimum for normal text. It is arithmetic, not opinion, which is why it settled the red question.
Cap height
The height of a capital letter. Stroke thickness gets specified as a percentage of it — here 24%, against roughly 12% in the 2013 logo.
Contact sheet
A grid of many options at small size, for comparing at a glance. Good for ranking execution, and — as round B found the hard way — bad for spotting ideas.
